items.title: 14.2.1 Dot or Scalar Product of Two Vectors and Its Geometrical Interpretation

blocks.text: We shall now consider products of two vectors that originated in the study of physics and engineering. The concept of angle between two vectors is expressed in terms of a scalar product of two vectors.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text: In physics a force \(\underline{F}\) moving a body through a displacement \(\underline{d}\) does work equal to \(|\underline{F}||\underline{d}|\cos\theta\), where \(\theta\) is the angle between them. Only the part of the force along the motion does the work. Mathematics gives this combination of two vectors a name: the dot product. Its answer is a number, which is why it is also called the scalar product.

Let two non-zero vectors \(\underline{u}\) and \(\underline{v}\), in the plane or in space, have some initial point. The dot product of \(\underline{u}\) and \(\underline{v}\), written as \(\underline{u} \cdot \underline{v}\), is defined by

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The book prints "have some initial point". It should be "have the same initial point": the angle between two vectors is measured when both start from the same point.

blocks.text_alt: u dot v equals the magnitude of u times the magnitude of v times cos theta

blocks.alt: Three drawings of vectors u and v drawn from the same point. In the first the angle theta between them is acute, in the second it is obtuse, and in the third u and v point in opposite directions so theta equals pi. A curved arrow marks theta in each.
blocks.caption: Figure: the angle θ between u and v, measured with both vectors starting at the same point (original drawing after the textbook's figure)

blocks.text: Where \(\theta\) in the angle between \(\underline{u}\) and \(\underline{v}\) and \(0 \le \theta \le \pi\).

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The book prints "Where θ in the angle". It should read "where θ is the angle".

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
How to read the definition:
1. Place the two vectors tail to tail (both starting at one point). If they are drawn head to tail, slide one of them first; otherwise you may measure \(\pi - \theta\) instead of \(\theta\).
2. \(\theta\) is always taken between \(0\) and \(\pi\) (\(0^{\circ}\) to \(180^{\circ}\)).
3. \(|\underline{u}|\) and \(|\underline{v}|\) are positive, so the sign of \(\underline{u} \cdot \underline{v}\) is the sign of \(\cos\theta\) (table below). The three drawings show the three cases.

blocks.caption: Our summary: the sign of the dot product

blocks.text: (a) If \(\underline{u} = a_{1}\underline{i} + b_{1}\underline{j}\) and \(\underline{v} = a_{2}\underline{i} + b_{2}\underline{j}\) are two non-zero vectors in the plane. The dot product \(\underline{u} \cdot \underline{v}\) is defined by:

blocks.text_alt: u dot v equals a 1 a 2 plus b 1 b 2

blocks.text: (b) If \(\underline{u} = a_{1}\underline{i} + b_{1}\underline{j} + c_{1}\underline{k}\) and \(\underline{v} = a_{2}\underline{i} + b_{2}\underline{j} + c_{2}\underline{k}\) are two non-zero vectors in space. The dot product \(\underline{u} \cdot \underline{v}\) is defined by

blocks.text_alt: u dot v equals a 1 a 2 plus b 1 b 2 plus c 1 c 2

blocks.title: Note
blocks.text: The dot product is also referred as the scalar product or the inner product.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Definition 2 is the working formula: multiply matching components and add. For example (ours), if \(\underline{u} = 2\underline{i} + 3\underline{j} - \underline{k}\) and \(\underline{v} = \underline{i} - \underline{j} + 4\underline{k}\), then
\[\underline{u} \cdot \underline{v} = (2)(1) + (3)(-1) + (-1)(4)\]
\[= 2 - 3 - 4 = -5\]
The answer is negative, so the angle between \(\underline{u}\) and \(\underline{v}\) is obtuse.
Definition 1 needs the angle; Definition 2 needs only the components. Example 5 proves (for the plane) that the two definitions always give the same number; 14.2.5 derives Definition 2 in space.

blocks.title: Example 5
blocks.problem:
Prove that equivalence of following two definitions of dot product of two vectors:
(i) If \(\underline{v} = [x_{1}, y_{1}]\) and \(\underline{w} = [x_{2}, y_{2}]\) are two vectors in the plane, then \(\underline{v} \cdot \underline{w} = x_{1}x_{2} + y_{1}y_{2}\)
(ii) If \(\underline{v}\) and \(\underline{w}\) are two non-zero vectors in the plane, then \(\underline{v} \cdot \underline{w} = |\underline{v}||\underline{w}|\cos\theta\), where \(\theta\) is the angle between \(\underline{v}\) and \(\underline{w}\) and \(0 \le \theta \le \pi\).
steps:
Given: \(\underline{v} = [x_{1}, y_{1}]\), \(\underline{w} = [x_{2}, y_{2}]\), non-zero, with angle \(\theta\) between them.
To prove: \(x_{1}x_{2} + y_{1}y_{2} = |\underline{v}||\underline{w}|\cos\theta\), so both definitions give the same number.
Method: put \(\underline{v}\) and \(\underline{w}\) as two sides of a triangle and use the law of cosines (from trigonometry) on the third side. The law of cosines contains \(\cos\theta\); writing the lengths in components brings in \(x_{1}x_{2} + y_{1}y_{2}\).

Step 1: Form a triangle
Draw \(\underline{v}\) and \(\underline{w}\) from the same point. The third side joins the tip of \(\underline{w}\) to the tip of \(\underline{v}\); it is the vector \(\underline{v} - \underline{w}\), and it lies opposite the angle \(\theta\).
Why: \(\underline{w} + (\underline{v} - \underline{w}) = \underline{v}\), so going along \(\underline{w}\) and then along \(\underline{v} - \underline{w}\) reaches the tip of \(\underline{v}\) (head-to-tail rule). Its length is \(|\underline{v} - \underline{w}|\).

Step 2: Law of cosines
\[|\underline{v} - \underline{w}|^{2} = |\underline{v}|^{2} + |\underline{w}|^{2}\]
\[- 2|\underline{v}||\underline{w}|\cos\theta \quad \text{...(1)}\]
Why: in any triangle (side opposite the angle)\(^{2}\) = (sum of the squares of the other two sides) \(- 2\)(product of those sides)\(\cos\)(angle).

Step 3: Write each length in components
\[\underline{v} - \underline{w} = [x_{1} - x_{2},\ y_{1} - y_{2}]\]
\[|\underline{v} - \underline{w}|^{2} = (x_{1} - x_{2})^{2} + (y_{1} - y_{2})^{2}\]
\[|\underline{v}|^{2} = x_{1}^{2} + y_{1}^{2},\quad |\underline{w}|^{2} = x_{2}^{2} + y_{2}^{2}\]
Why: vectors are subtracted component by component, and the square of a magnitude is the sum of the squares of the components.

Step 4: Substitute into (1)
\[(x_{1} - x_{2})^{2} + (y_{1} - y_{2})^{2}\]
\[= (x_{1}^{2} + y_{1}^{2}) + (x_{2}^{2} + y_{2}^{2})\]
\[- 2|\underline{v}||\underline{w}|\cos\theta\]
Why: this turns the geometric equation (1) into an equation in the components.

Step 5: Expand and cancel
Left side:
\[x_{1}^{2} - 2x_{1}x_{2} + x_{2}^{2} + y_{1}^{2} - 2y_{1}y_{2} + y_{2}^{2}\]
The squares \(x_{1}^{2}, x_{2}^{2}, y_{1}^{2}, y_{2}^{2}\) appear on both sides and cancel:
\[-2x_{1}x_{2} - 2y_{1}y_{2} = -2|\underline{v}||\underline{w}|\cos\theta\]
Why: \((a - b)^{2} = a^{2} - 2ab + b^{2}\); equal terms on the two sides of an equation can be removed.

Step 6: Divide by \(-2\)
\[x_{1}x_{2} + y_{1}y_{2} = |\underline{v}||\underline{w}|\cos\theta\]
\[= \underline{v} \cdot \underline{w}\]
Why: dividing both sides by the same non-zero number keeps the equation true. The left side is definition (i) and the right side is definition (ii).

Check:
Take \(\underline{v} = [1, 0]\) and \(\underline{w} = [1, 1]\); the angle between them is \(45^{\circ}\).
\[x_{1}x_{2} + y_{1}y_{2} = 1 + 0 = 1\]
\[|\underline{v}||\underline{w}|\cos 45^{\circ} = 1 \cdot \sqrt{2} \cdot \tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} = 1\]
Both definitions give \(1\).

blocks.alt: A triangle. Vector v runs along the base from the common starting point, vector w goes up from the same point making angle theta with v, and the third side, labelled v minus w, runs from the tip of w to the tip of v.
blocks.caption: Figure: the triangle formed by v, w and v − w (Example 5) (original drawing after the textbook's figure)

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: In the book's figure for Example 5 the arrowhead on the side labelled \(\underline{v} - \underline{w}\) points from the tip of \(\underline{v}\) towards the tip of \(\underline{w}\); that direction is \(\underline{w} - \underline{v}\). Since \(\underline{w} + (\underline{v} - \underline{w}) = \underline{v}\), the vector \(\underline{v} - \underline{w}\) goes from the tip of \(\underline{w}\) to the tip of \(\underline{v}\), as in our drawing. The length \(|\underline{v} - \underline{w}|\), which the proof uses, is the same either way.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
1. \(\underline{u} \cdot \underline{v} = |\underline{u}||\underline{v}|\cos\theta\), with the vectors tail to tail and \(0 \le \theta \le \pi\).
2. In components: \(\underline{u} \cdot \underline{v} = a_{1}a_{2} + b_{1}b_{2} + c_{1}c_{2}\).
3. The answer is a scalar; another name is the inner product.
4. Sign: positive for an acute angle, zero for a right angle, negative for an obtuse angle.
5. The two definitions are equivalent (Example 5, by the law of cosines).

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text:
1. Multiplying the components but forgetting to add them: \(\underline{u} \cdot \underline{v}\) is one number, not \(2\underline{i} - 3\underline{j} - 4\underline{k}\).
2. Losing a negative sign: \((3)(-1) = -3\). Write every product in brackets.
3. Measuring the angle with the vectors head to tail, which gives \(\pi - \theta\).
